notable_claims: Possession of a password cracking program alone may lead to threats against a student's computer account privileges.
Some academic institutions consider leaving class files unprotected (via umask) as potentially providing solutions to assignments, violating academic integrity.
Debates existed over whether 'offensive' or 'intimidating' speech on university bulletin boards should be quantified or suppressed.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several early 1990s disputes regarding computer use in academic settings. Key issues include the possession of password-cracking software, the ethics of file permissions (umask) and academic integrity, and the boundaries of acceptable speech on university bulletin boards.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.07

notable_claims: Possession of a password cracking program led to administrative scrutiny and account revocation for some students.
University administration viewed the presence of such tools as evidence of unethical behavior regardless of whether they were executed.
organizations: The Indiana Academy for Science, Mathematics, and the Humanities
classification.summary: Bryan Strawser reports that his university's Unix system administrator updated the message of the day (MOTD) to warn against password hacking after discovering a password cracking program on several accounts. Strawser argues that he only possessed the software for research purposes into computer security and had not executed it on the university system. He expresses concern over being penalized for the mere possession of security tools, comparing it to the role of a locksmith.
classification.title: Article 1--(none)

notable_claims: University students should not be expelled from computer systems without a hearing.
The Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students protects student status pending final disciplinary action.
classification.summary: Bryan Strawser reports that a university system administrator issued a warning via the message of the day and revoked user accounts based on suspected impropriety. Carl Kadie responds by arguing that students should not be denied computer access without due process or a hearing. Kadie cites the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students to support the need for procedural fairness.
classification.title: Article 2--Re: (none)

notable_claims: Jewish students claimed that publishing Holocaust denial in a student paper constitutes racial harassment.
The OSU Office of Affirmative Action has the authority to discipline students up to expulsion.
classification.summary: A report and commentary on a controversy at Ohio State University after the student newspaper, The Lantern, published Holocaust revisionist content as an editorial. Jewish students filed complaints with the Office of Affirmative Action, arguing the content constituted racial harassment. The author argues that attempting to discipline the editors undermines academic freedom and critical thinking.
classification.title: Another OSU Lantern Imbroglio

notable_claims: Extracts of computer crime statutes were made available for upload/download.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie notified the group about new uploads containing extracts of computer crime statutes. The announcement was cross-posted to several newsgroups, including alt.bbs.allsysop.

notable_claims: The SULAW archive hosted a collection of international and US state-level computer crime statutes for public access in 1992.
classification.summary: Mark Neely announced the upload of various computer crime statute extracts to the SULAW archive. The collection includes criminal codes from numerous US states, Canada, the United Kingdom, and a proposed law for Ghana. These documents provide primary legal texts regarding unauthorized access and computer fraud.
classification.title: Article 5--New Uploads (Computer Crime Statutes extracts)

notable_claims: Anti-Semitic content was identified on a large computer network.
classification.summary: This item is a pointer to a discussion from the comp.org.eff.talk newsgroup regarding the discovery of anti-Semitic content on a large computer network. It highlights early concerns over hate speech and moderation on distributed digital networks.
classification.title: Anti-Semitism Found on Large Computer Network

identity.subject: Article 6--[comp.org.eff.talk]  "Anti-Semitism Found on Large Computer Network"

notable_claims: Anti-Semitic material was being distributed via the Internet from various academic and corporate nodes.
The ADL explicitly stated they did not advocate for censorship of the Internet despite the presence of hate speech.
UC Berkeley's policies on computer expression were described as too general to support specific legal action against the content.
classification.summary: A report detailing the discovery of anti-Semitic and Holocaust-revisionist material on the early Internet by a UC Berkeley student. The item highlights the tension between hate speech and censorship, noting that while private networks like Prodigy censored such content, the ADL declined to request similar action on the Internet to avoid advocating for censorship.
classification.title: Anti-Semitism Found on Large Computer Network

identity.subject: Article 7--"Anti-Semitism Found on Large Computer Network"

notable_claims: An institutional ban on games was implemented or proposed in the cso.general environment.
classification.summary: A discussion post regarding a ban on games within a computing environment. The item reflects early institutional conflicts over the acceptable use of shared academic computing resources.
classification.title: Re: Game Ban!!! (What the...?)

notable_claims: Prior to the ban, up to 80% of computers in Illini Hall were occupied by gamers.
Students seeking academic work often leave labs if they see all terminals occupied, even if those terminals are being used for games.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding a ban on gaming in computer labs at the University of Illinois. The participants argue that gamers intimidate other students and occupy resources needed for academic work, justifying the restriction to ensure availability for classwork.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: Game Ban!!! (What the...?)

notable_claims: A TA suggested that knowingly making class files world-readable could be viewed as providing solutions to assignments under a Code of Academic Integrity.
classification.summary: Eric Scheirer discusses a conversation with a TA regarding whether setting a permissive umask (022) in UNIX constitutes a violation of academic integrity. The concern was that making programming assignments world-readable could be interpreted as providing solutions to other students. Scheirer questions if such policies are formally codified or enforced at other institutions.
classification.title: Article 10--umask & culpability

notable_claims: A student at Cornell was told that using 'umask 022' might violate the Code of Academic Integrity.
At Dartmouth, leaving files unprotected is generally not a punishable offense unless it is proven the user intended for others to copy them for academic benefit.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding whether setting a permissive 'umask' (allowing others to read files) constitutes a violation of academic integrity. The exchange compares the policies of Cornell University and Dartmouth College regarding user responsibility for file security versus student complicity in cheating.
classification.title: Article 11--Re: umask & culpability

notable_claims: A TA suggested that setting umask 022 could be a violation of Cornell's Code of Academic Integrity if it allows others to peruse programming solutions.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding whether setting a permissive UNIX umask (022) constitutes a violation of academic integrity by making assignment solutions available to others. The participants debate the analogy between file permissions and unlocked physical rooms, questioning if 'knowingly' leaving files readable equals providing unauthorized help. The exchange highlights early tensions between technical openness/sharing and institutional codes of conduct.
classification.title: Article 12--Re: umask & culpability

notable_claims: Questions the legal and practical distinction between offensive, intimidating, and harassing speech in a digital context.
classification.summary: David Marc Nieporent critiques the justification for suppressing speech on Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) computer bulletin boards. He challenges the distinction between 'offensive' and 'harassing' speech and questions the evidence of actual harm caused by such communications.
classification.title: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

identity.subject: Article 13--Re: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards

notable_claims: Questions whether non-physical speech can pose a 'clear and imminent danger'
Argues that defining harassing speech is difficult to do without violating general speech policies
classification.summary: Mike Percy responds to a debate regarding speech restrictions on Carnegie Mellon University's computer bulletin boards. He challenges the distinction between 'offensive' speech and 'harassing' speech, questioning how such boundaries can be quantified or enforced without violating free speech policies.
classification.title: Speech restrictions on CMU computer bboards
